title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: "Here it comes again! Again I see it all!" Anna said to herself, the moment the carriage moved off and, swaying lightly, began rumbling over the little paving stones of the road, and once again one impression chased rapidly after another.

"Yes — what was the last thing I was thinking about so clearly?" she tried to remember. "'_Tiutkin, coiffeur?_' — no, not that. Yes, what Yashvin says, that the struggle for existence and hatred are the one thing that holds people together. No, it's a useless trip you're making," she said in her head to a party in a coach and four, evidently off on an outing in the country. "And the dog you're taking along will be no use to you. You can't get away from yourselves." Turning her eyes in the direction Pyotr had glanced, she saw a factory worker who was almost dead drunk, his head hanging, being led off by a policeman. "There — he's found a quicker way," she thought. "Count Vronsky and I didn't find that happiness either, even though we expected so much from it." And now, for the first time, Anna turned the glaring light in which she was seeing everything onto her relationship with him, which she had been avoiding thinking about until now. "What was he looking for in me? Not love so much as the gratification of vanity." She remembered his words, the expression on his face, like an abject setter, in the early days of their affair. And everything now confirmed it. "Yes, there was the thrill of conquest in him. Of course there was love too, but the main element was the pride of having pulled it off. He showed me off. Now that's over. There's nothing to be proud of. Not to be proud of, but to be ashamed of. He's taken from me everything he could, and now I'm no use to him. He's tired of me, and he's trying not to behave dishonorably toward me. He let it slip yesterday — he wants the divorce and the marriage so he can burn his bridges. He loves me, but how? The zest is gone, as the English say. That fellow there wants everyone to admire him and is very pleased with himself," she thought, looking at a red-faced clerk riding a riding-school horse. "Yes, there's no flavor left in me for him now. If I leave him, deep down he'll be glad."
This wasn't just a guess; she saw it distinctly in the piercing light that was now revealing the meaning of life and of human relationships to her.

"My love keeps growing more passionate and selfish, while his keeps fading and fading, and that's why we're drifting apart." She went on thinking. "And there's no helping it. He is everything for me, and I want him more and more to give himself over to me completely. And he wants more and more to get away from me. We walked toward each other right up to the point of falling in love, and ever since we've been irresistibly drifting in opposite directions. And nothing can change that. He tells me I'm insanely jealous, and I've told myself the same thing; but it isn't true. I'm not jealous, I'm dissatisfied. But...." She parted her lips and shifted in her seat in the excitement of the thought that had just struck her. "If only I could be something other than a mistress, caring passionately about nothing but his caresses; but I can't, and I don't want to be anything else. And by that very wanting I provoke disgust in him, and he provokes rage in me, and it can't be any different. Don't I know that he wouldn't deceive me, that he has no designs on Princess Sorokina, that he isn't in love with Kitty, that he won't desert me! I know all that, but it doesn't make it any better. If, without loving me, he treats me well and kindly out of _duty_, and doesn't give me what I want, that's a thousand times worse than unkindness! That's — hell! And that's exactly how it is. For a long time now he hasn't loved me. And where love ends, hate begins. I don't know these streets at all. Hills, it seems, and still houses and more houses.... And in the houses, always people and more people.... How many of them, no end of them, and all hating each other! Come on, let me try to think what it would take to make me happy. Well? Suppose I get a divorce, and Alexey Alexandrovitch lets me have Seryozha, and I marry Vronsky." Thinking of Alexey Alexandrovitch, she at once pictured him with extraordinary clarity, as if he were alive in front of her, with his mild, lifeless, dull eyes, the blue veins on his white hands, his intonations and the cracking of his fingers, and remembering the feeling that had existed between them, which had also been called love, she shuddered with revulsion. "All right, I'm divorced, and I become Vronsky's wife. Well, will Kitty stop looking at me the way she looked at me today? No. And will Seryozha stop asking about and wondering at my two husbands? And is there any new feeling I could awaken between Vronsky and me? Is there any chance, if not of happiness, then at least of some relief from misery? No, no!" she answered now without any hesitation at all. "Impossible! Life is pulling us apart, and I'm the cause of his unhappiness and he of mine, and there's no changing him or me. Every attempt has been made — the screw has been stripped. Oh, a beggar woman with a baby. She thinks I'll feel sorry for her. Aren't we all just flung into the world to hate each other, and so to torture ourselves and each other? Schoolboys coming — laughing Seryozha?" she thought. "I imagined I loved him too, and used to be moved by my own tenderness. But I've lived without him, I traded him for another love, and didn't regret the trade until that love was satisfied." And with disgust she thought about what she had meant by that love. And the clarity with which she now saw life, her own and everyone else's, was a pleasure to her. "It's the same with me and Pyotr, and the coachman Fyodor, and that merchant, and all the people living along the Volga where those posters invite you to go, and everywhere, and always," she thought, just as she had pulled in under the low-pitched roof of the Nizhigorod station and the porters came running to meet her.
She had completely forgotten where she was going and why, and only with great effort grasped the question.
"Yes," she said, handing him her purse, and taking a little red bag in her hand, she got out of the carriage.

Pushing her way through the crowd to the first-class waiting room, she gradually remembered every detail of her situation, and the plans she was wavering between. And once again, in the same old sore spots, hope and then despair poisoned the wounds of her tortured, fearfully hammering heart. Sitting on the star-shaped sofa waiting for the train, she looked with disgust at the people coming and going (they were all hateful to her) and thought about how she would get to the station, how she would write him a note, what she would write, and how he was right now complaining to his mother about his position, not understanding her suffering, and how she would walk into the room and what she would say. Then she thought that life might still be happy, and how miserably she loved and hated him, and how terribly her heart was pounding.
